Flabbergasted

/FLAB-er-gas-tid/ - the stress falls on FLAB · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Flabbergasted means utterly astounded.

The plumber cut into the kitchen wall to trace a leak and stood flabbergasted: behind the plaster ran a painted 1920s mural, intact from floor to ceiling.

Worked Example

At the retirement dinner, the school's soft-spoken janitor rose to give the customary two-minute farewell. Instead he announced that he had been saving quietly for thirty years and was donating fifty thousand dollars to rebuild the library. The room sat flabbergasted — forks down, mouths open — for a long moment before the applause hit.

Flabbergasted is far stronger than 'surprised': it means utterly astounded, knocked right past speech. You are surprised by a pop quiz; you are flabbergasted when the quiz is handed out by the superintendent, in costume, on live television.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

dumbfounded: Dumbfounded zooms in on one symptom of shock: the words stop coming, and you stand there with nothing to say. Flabbergasted names the whole state — utterly astounded by something almost past believing. A hard riddle can leave you dumbfounded; flabbergasted needs real news, a jaw-dropper that upends what you thought you knew.

stunned: Stunned means knocked briefly out of the ability to react — by news or by a blow — so that for a moment you cannot respond. Flabbergasted is bigger and louder: utterly astounded by something you can scarcely believe. A stunned person freezes for a beat; a flabbergasted one can hardly accept what just happened.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

calm: steady and untroubled by the news

unsurprised: having seen it coming all along

Where it sits · how hard the shock hits — surprised → astonished → flabbergasted

surprised vs. flabbergasted: Surprised is the everyday word — an unexpected knock surprises you — and it sits far below flabbergasted.

astonished vs. flabbergasted: Astonished goes further than surprised, striking real wonder, but it stops short of flabbergasted, which leaves you gaping with nothing to say.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — flabbergast

Root — flabbergast: to astound utterly (English slang of unknown origin)

Suffix — -ed

Suffix — -ed: put into that state

Put it together

Put it together: Flabbergast (to astound utterly) + -ed = put into an utterly astounded state. There is nothing older to peel off: flabbergast surfaced in 1772 in a magazine's list of fashionable new slang, perhaps mashing 'flabby' and 'aghast' together, but its inventor and its parts were never recorded.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Flabbergast arrived as ready-made slang in the 1770s — a London magazine listed it among the year's new vogue words — and whatever was mashed together to coin it was never written down. It has no traceable root and therefore no cousins; the word stands alone.

Strength Check

Word Choice

informal / vivid

Flabbergasted is conversational and a little theatrical — perfect in speech and light prose for total astonishment. In formal writing, astounded or astonished carries the same weight with a straighter face. And do not spend it on mild surprises; a word this loud needs a shock its own size.
